C0.quote: counting variants of Swap- and ShiftBribery
C0.note: Computational (counting) complexity of bribery in voting rules, plus robustness experiments.

C1.note: Main results are complexity theorems; experiments on synthetic and cycling data are also reported. Counting bribery is related to SB.

C2.1.quote: we sometimes refer to preference orders as votes

C2.2.quote: Each voter vi has a preference order, which ranks all candidates

C2.3.quote: some voter would have ranked two candidates differently
C2.3.note: Introduction mentions voters who viewed candidates as similar or lacked information, i.e. held attitudes outside the formal model; the formal model uses only preference orders.

C2.4.quote: Each voter vi has a preference order, which ranks all candidates
C2.4.note: Preference orders are described as voters' preferences and the rule applied directly; no statement about submission vs. held attitude. The intro mentions possible misranking, which only informally suggests errors.

C3.1.note: No voters are modelled as strategic; bribery changes votes externally and the swaps are random.

C3.2.note: No statement that voters submit their held attitude.

C4.1.note: No utility-type notions for voters are used.

C5.1.note: Robustness of winners is evaluated, not welfare, efficiency, representation or distortion.

VOT.note: Voters take no action in the model; swaps are applied by the briber or at random.

BRI.quote_behav: We ask if there is an election E 0 where p is an R-winner
BRI.quote_info: we are given an election E, a designated candidate p, and a budget r
BRI.note: The briber is the Swap-/Shift-Bribery decision problem agent seeking to make p win; full knowledge of the election is implicit in the input. Counting variants count the ways to achieve the goal.

C8.1.quote: We ask if there is an election E 0 where p is an R-winner
C8.1.note: Bribery is a decision/optimisation problem about the existence of actions achieving a goal.

C9.2.note: For the practical robustness claim to follow, one needs the random-swap model to reflect real voter errors or uncertainty, and a relation between votes and voters' held opinions. The latter is not stated; the intro only informally mentions misranking.
